reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AABB Technical Manual
clinicalPearls: Protein C is a vitamin K-dependent natural anticoagulant that, once activated, inactivates factors Va and VIIIa; its deficiency is a strong inherited thrombophilia
Heterozygous deficiency causes venous thromboembolism, often beginning in young adulthood and sometimes provoked by additional risk factors
Homozygous or compound heterozygous deficiency presents in the newborn period with purpura fulminans, a life-threatening microvascular thrombotic emergency
Starting a vitamin K antagonist without concurrent heparin-type cover can precipitate skin necrosis, because protein C levels fall faster than the procoagulant factors
Levels are lowered by acute thrombosis, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, and vitamin K antagonist therapy, so timing of testing is critical
Both functional (activity) and antigenic assays are used to distinguish reduced production from a dysfunctional protein
Confirmation ideally requires repeat testing away from the acute event and off vitamin K antagonists, with family studies where appropriate
reference.pathophysiology: Protein C circulates as an inactive precursor and is activated on the endothelial surface by the thrombin-thrombomodulin complex. Activated protein C, with its cofactor protein S, proteolytically inactivates factors Va and VIIIa, thereby limiting thrombin generation. Inherited deficiency, whether from reduced synthesis (type I) or a functionally impaired protein (type II), removes this brake and shifts haemostasis toward thrombosis. The short half-life of protein C explains the transient hypercoagulable window at the start of vitamin K antagonist therapy, when protein C is depleted before the longer-lived procoagulant factors, producing the risk of skin necrosis.
additionalDifferentials: Factor V Leiden and prothrombin variant
Disseminated intravascular coagulation causing acquired protein C consumption
additionalInvestigations: Functional protein C activity assay as the primary test
Protein C antigen level to classify the deficiency type
Repeat testing away from acute thrombosis and off vitamin K antagonists
Family studies and genetic testing where results will guide management
redFlags: Neonatal purpura fulminans indicating severe homozygous deficiency and requiring emergency treatment
Skin necrosis developing after initiation of a vitamin K antagonist
Extensive or recurrent venous thromboembolism at a young age
Widespread microvascular thrombosis suggesting an acute prothrombotic crisis
reference.prognosis: Heterozygous carriers have a good prognosis with appropriate management of thrombotic events and high-risk periods, whereas homozygous deficiency presenting with neonatal purpura fulminans is life-threatening and requires urgent replacement and long-term anticoagulation.
pitfalls: Diagnosing deficiency from levels drawn during acute thrombosis or vitamin K antagonist therapy
Initiating a vitamin K antagonist without overlapping parenteral anticoagulation, risking skin necrosis
Confusing acquired causes such as liver disease or DIC with inherited deficiency
Failing to repeat and confirm a low result before committing to lifelong conclusions
management: Treat acute venous thromboembolism with anticoagulation, starting heparin such as low-molecular-weight heparin and overlapping before introducing any vitamin K antagonist
Never begin a vitamin K antagonist without concurrent heparin cover, to avoid warfarin-induced skin necrosis from the rapid fall in protein C
Individualise the duration of anticoagulation, favouring extended treatment after unprovoked or recurrent thrombosis, using a DOAC or a vitamin K antagonist
Treat neonatal purpura fulminans as an emergency with protein C concentrate or fresh frozen plasma replacement alongside anticoagulation
Provide thromboprophylaxis during high-risk periods such as surgery, immobility and pregnancy, and counsel against oestrogen-containing contraception
Offer family testing and genetic counselling, and confirm the diagnosis with repeat testing away from acute thrombosis and off vitamin K antagonists
